query: For titanium alloys used as structural materials, formulate one hypothesis for an intervention that could increase surface hardness and wear resistance. Specify the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to the untreated alloy, the service or test conditions under which the effect should hold, prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a controlled experiment with clear results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A two‐step surface modification combining low‐temperature plasma nitriding in a mixed NH3/N2 atmosphere to form a hard, compressively stressed Ti‐N compound layer, followed by a low-energy laser surface polishing step to reduce nitriding‐induced roughness, will yield a Ti-6Al-4V alloy with significantly higher surface hardness and superior wear resistance under cyclic and sliding wear conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: As-received Ti-6Al-4V alloy with typical Widmanstätten or equiaxed microstructure and baseline hardness around 350 HV.
generation.intervention: First, perform plasma nitriding at 750 °C for 4 hours using an NH3:N2 gas mixture (with a ratio of 1:2) to develop a multi-phase Ti-N layer (containing δ-TiN and ε-Ti2N) with residual compressive stresses. Second, apply a controlled, low-energy laser surface polishing (or low-power laser remelting) process to decrease the post-nitriding surface roughness without substantially altering the nitrided layer.
generation.conditions: Laboratory wear tests under both dry sliding and moderate cyclic loading conditions at ambient temperature, with applied loads in the range of 5-8 N (similar to standard pin-on-disk testing conditions).
generation.structural_mediator: The plasma nitriding forms a thin (~2-4 µm) hard compound layer enriched in TiN and Ti2N that increases surface hardness and produces compressive residual stress. The subsequent laser polishing smooths the surface, reducing asperities and mitigating premature wear or stress concentration sites.
generation.mechanism: The nitriding step increases the resistance of the alloy to plastic deformation and hinders dislocation motion due to the formation of high-hardness Ti-nitrides. However, nitriding typically increases surface roughness, which can undermine wear resistance at high sliding speeds. By combining this with a laser polishing step that removes or reduces surface peaks and valleys without compromising the integrity of the nitrided layer, the modified surface can retain high hardness while also benefiting from a smoother, more uniform contact interface that minimizes abrasive stress and wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with the untreated Ti-6Al-4V alloy, the modified surface is expected to exhibit a 300-400% increase in surface hardness (potentially reaching >1400 HV) and a significant reduction in wear rate (possibly by a factor of about 2 or more compared with nitriding alone).
generation.baseline: Untreated Ti-6Al-4V alloy typically shows lower hardness (~350 HV) and higher wear rates under cyclic and dry sliding conditions.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected under moderate wear and fatigue conditions typical for structural applications; however, under extreme loads or very high cycle interactions, potential delamination of the nitrided layer or the effect of laser polishing on layer adhesion might become critical factors.
generation.uncertainty: While existing studies (e.g., PMC6384831::web::015::3_results_and_discussions and PMC6356806::web::020::3_5_friction_and_wear_testing_analysis) support the beneficial effects of plasma nitriding for increasing hardness and wear resistance and show that surface texturing or secondary treatments can reduce friction, it remains uncertain how well a low-energy laser polishing step will preserve the integrity of the nitrided layer and exactly how much additional wear reduction can be achieved over nitriding alone. The transfer of these effects from fatigue behavior improvements in nitriding studies to wear resistance improvements with laser polishing is novel in this hypothesis.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of Ti-6Al-4V alloy samples: (A) untreated, (B) samples subject only to plasma nitriding at 750 °C for 4 h in an NH3:N2 (1:2) atmosphere, and (C) samples that undergo the combined treatment (plasma nitriding as in B followed by a low-energy laser polishing step). Conduct standardized pin-on-disk wear tests and hardness measurements (micro-Vickers) on all sets. Surface roughness should be quantified using profilometry, and microstructural integrity of the nitrided layer should be verified via SEM and XRD.
measurements: Surface roughness (Ra) before and after laser polishing
SEM imaging and XRD phase analysis of the treated layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the combined treatment samples (C) do not show a statistically significant increase in hardness (targeting over 1400 HV) and a lower wear rate (at least 50% reduction in wear volume compared both to untreated samples and to nitrided-only samples) while also exhibiting reduced surface roughness compared to nitrided-only samples (B), then the hypothesis is falsified.

This is in agreement with another study by Rodriguez et al. []. According to Farokhzadeh et al. [], the nitride layer reduces the extent of brittle failure on the specimen surface while the diffusion zone provides mechanical support. As per the study of Morita et al [], the formation of these layers after plasma nitriding increases the surface hardness of the alloy, which in turn increases the resistance to movement of dislocations and, as a consequence, increases the fatigue strength of the alloy. The effect of thermohydrogen treatment and vacuum ion–plasma nitriding on the determination of the volume and surface structure of ball heads made of Ti–6Al–4V alloy was studied. It was found that the submicrocrystalline structure formed in the head during thermohydrogen treatment makes it possible to achieve hardness values of 39–41 units HRC and a surface roughness of 0.02 μm. It was shown that the creation of a modified layer consisting of ε (TiN) and δ (Ti2N) titanium nitrides on the surface of a ball head and the solid interstitial solution of nitrogen in α-titanium makes it possible to completely eliminate material wear when testing for friction on ultra-high-molecular-weight polyethylene. The equivalent analysis was also conducted with a ball head that had been implanted in a human body for 12 years. It was found that the change in the color of the head, from slightly golden after nitriding to metallic, is due to the formation of an oxynitride nanoscale layer on the surface. It was shown that in contrast with films made of titanium oxide, the film developed in this study has high wear resistance.
